title: Transaction Isolation Levels and Anomalies
lesson:
Isolation is the 'I' in ACID: it defines how much concurrently running transactions can see of each other's work. Perfect isolation (serializability, where the outcome equals some serial execution) is expensive, so databases offer weaker levels that trade correctness guarantees for throughput. The SQL standard defines levels by which anomalies they forbid.

The classic anomalies: a dirty read sees another transaction's uncommitted write; a non-repeatable read happens when you read the same row twice and get different values because someone committed in between; a phantom read happens when re-running a range query returns new or missing rows. READ UNCOMMITTED allows all three, READ COMMITTED forbids dirty reads, REPEATABLE READ additionally forbids non-repeatable reads, and SERIALIZABLE forbids phantoms as well. READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL and many other databases.

The standard's list is incomplete. Snapshot-based implementations of REPEATABLE READ (such as PostgreSQL's) still permit write skew: two transactions each read an overlapping set of rows, make disjoint writes based on what they read, and both commit, breaking an invariant. The classic example is two on-call doctors each checking that at least one other doctor is on call and then both going off call. Lost updates (read-modify-write races) are another anomaly that plain READ COMMITTED allows unless you use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, atomic updates, or version checks.

Choosing a level is a per-workload decision. Use the default for most reads and writes, take explicit row locks or atomic updates for hot read-modify-write paths, and use SERIALIZABLE where invariants span multiple rows, accepting that the database may abort transactions with serialization failures, so the application must be ready to retry them.

questions.prompt: A transaction reads a row twice and sees different committed values because another transaction committed between the reads. What is this anomaly?
questions.explanation: Seeing a different committed value for the same row within one transaction is a non-repeatable read.

questions.prompt: Order these standard isolation levels from weakest to strongest.
questions.explanation: Each level forbids more anomalies than the one before it, ending with serializable.

questions.prompt: A snapshot-isolation-based REPEATABLE READ level can still allow write skew.
questions.explanation: Snapshot isolation only detects conflicting writes to the same rows, so disjoint writes based on overlapping reads can both commit.

questions.prompt: When a database runs transactions at SERIALIZABLE and detects a conflict, it may abort one with a serialization failure, so the application must ____ the transaction.
questions.explanation: Serialization failures are expected under strict isolation and are resolved by retrying the aborted transaction.

questions.prompt: Which fix best prevents a lost update on a counter that app code reads, increments, and writes back under READ COMMITTED?
options: Use an atomic UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1 or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Retry the read until it matches
questions.explanation: Atomic updates or row locks make the read-modify-write a single protected step so concurrent writers cannot overwrite each other.
